chunks: When differential signaling is used. The question: When are they often used?
Differential signaling sends a signal as the difference between two wires.
Engineers use it when the signal has to survive noise, differences in ground voltage, or very high speed, or when the wires must not radiate much interference.
Short, slow connections between nearby chips usually stay single-ended because they do not need the extra wire.
Picture a 100 m cable running through a factory past motors and welders. Each throws interference at the cable.
With a twisted pair, the two wires sit almost in the same place, so the interference lands on both of them nearly equally.
The receiver reads only the difference between the wires, so it barely notices. A single wire in that cable would pick up the full interference with nothing to cancel it.
Each branch is a problem; each leaf is where differential signalling shows up. Many interfaces solve several at once.
Differential pair: two wires carrying opposite signals, read as a difference ("What a differential pair is and how it works").
Noise: unwanted voltage from motors, radios or other circuits.
Ground offset: the ground at one end of a long cable can sit at a different voltage from the ground at the other end.
Common-mode rejection: a receiver's ability to ignore what both wires share ("How differential signals improve noise immunity").
EMI: unwanted radio-frequency energy that a circuit gives off or picks up.
Two machines on a factory floor talk over an RS-485 link, a standard for long industrial cables. One drives at least 1. 5 volts between the two wires.
Their grounds differ by 3 volts, so both wires sit 3 volts higher at the far end. The difference is still 1. 5 volts.
The receiver accepts shifts from -7 volts to +12 volts, so it still reads the data correctly. A single-ended 3.
3 volts signal with a 3 volts ground shift would be badly corrupted. That is the whole idea: pay for a second wire when noise, ground differences or speed are the problem.
"Differential signalling is used wherever noise, ground offset, speed or EMI matter. Long cables and different grounds: RS-485, CAN, Ethernet.
High-speed links: USB, PCIe, SATA, HDMI, LVDS, where small differential swings give low EMI.
Low-level analog: balanced microphone lines and sensor bridges, where the signal is tiny and noise is common-mode. And precision ADC inputs and clocks.
I would not bother for short, slow on-board nets like GPIO or I2C."
